lesson.title: A Common Language for Numbers: SI Units in Chemistry
lesson.summary: This section introduces the SI base units and metric prefixes chemists rely on, and works through a unit conversion using dimensional analysis.
lesson.body:
The previous section established that a measurement is only useful if it can be trusted and compared, and that trust depends on everyone using the same defined units. Chemists worldwide rely on the International System of Units, abbreviated SI from its French name, Systeme International, a standardized set of units built around seven base units, five of which come up constantly in chemistry: the meter (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, the second (s) for time, the kelvin (K) for temperature, and the mole (mol) for amount of substance. Every other unit used in chemistry, no matter how specialized, is either one of these base units or built from some combination of them, which is what makes SI a genuinely unified system rather than a loose collection of separately defined units.

Some SI units are not base units themselves but are derived from combinations of the base units, and several of these derived units appear throughout chemistry. The liter, used constantly for volume, is derived from the meter, since one liter equals exactly 1000 cubic centimeters, a cube 10 centimeters on each edge. The joule, the SI unit of energy, is derived from mass, length, and time combined. Temperature deserves special mention because chemistry uses the kelvin scale rather than Celsius for most calculations, since kelvin starts at absolute zero, the coldest physically possible temperature, rather than at the freezing point of water; converting between them just requires adding 273.15 to a Celsius value to get kelvin, so 25 degrees Celsius, roughly room temperature, equals 298.15 K.

To make SI units convenient across the enormous range of scales chemistry deals with, from the diameter of an atom to the mass of a beaker of liquid, the system uses a standard set of prefixes that multiply or divide a base unit by powers of ten. Kilo means 1000 times the base unit, so a kilogram is 1000 grams. Centi means one hundredth, so a centimeter is one hundredth of a meter, and milli means one thousandth, so a milliliter is one thousandth of a liter. On the smaller end, chemists frequently use the prefix nano, one billionth, when describing atomic and molecular scale distances; a typical atom has a radius on the order of tenths of a nanometer. Because every prefix scales by a known power of ten, converting between them is always a matter of moving a decimal point rather than applying some unrelated conversion factor.

Working comfortably with SI prefixes requires converting between them accurately, and the standard tool for this is dimensional analysis, multiplying a measurement by a conversion factor written as a fraction equal to one, so that the unwanted unit cancels out. As a worked example, suppose a chemist measures 250 milligrams of a compound and needs that mass in grams for a calculation that expects SI base units. Since 1 gram equals 1000 milligrams, the conversion factor of 1 g over 1000 mg is multiplied by the given measurement: 250 mg times one gram per 1000 mg equals 0.250 g, with the milligram units canceling to leave grams. The same logic extends to more complex conversions built from several factors chained together, and it is this consistent, cancel the units approach, built on the standardized meter, kilogram, second, kelvin, and mole, that lets any measurement made anywhere in the world be reliably reproduced, compared, and trusted, closing the loop back to the scientific method's requirement that every claim rest on evidence others can independently verify.
